# Psalm 119:60–88: Research notes

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**Background (Heth, vv. 57–64; Teth, vv. 65–72).** David Guzik calls Psalm 119 a "string of pearls": each section looks at God's word from a different angle. He draws heavily on older writers such as Spurgeon, Clarke, Bridges and Poole. He also says the psalmist's claims to obey God are not boasting. They are made humbly, and they rest on God's mercy, not on his own merit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Precept Austin points out a memory trick in the Teth section (vv. 65–72). Begin verse 67 with "'Til" and verse 71 with "'Tis," and every line in English starts with "T," copying the Hebrew letter teth. It calls this stanza a study of life's hard lessons and how God uses hardship to help believers grow. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary

**v. 60:** Keil & Delitzsch: once the psalmist had examined his ways (v. 59), he quickly and gladly decided to keep God's word. He didn't argue it over with "flesh and blood," even with wicked men setting snares around him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): he didn't delay. Sinners should hurry to escape, and believers should be just as quick to glorify God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm

**v. 61:** Keil & Delitzsch take the Hebrew word to mean "snares" or "bonds" (compare v. 110), not "bands" of men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Coffman notes that Delitzsch read this verse together with v. 110 to mean the psalmist was in prison. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-62.html
- Guzik groups vv. 61–62 as faithfulness to God's word in hard times. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Matthew Henry (Concise): no worry or grief should push God's word out of our minds or block its comfort. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm

**v. 62:** Guzik: the psalmist put devotion to God ahead of sleep, giving up a good thing to seek God. Getting out of bed to praise shows reverence even in private, because praise involves the body as well as the soul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Barnes: the Hebrew literally means "the halving of the night." His mind was so full of God's law that he couldn't sleep and got up to praise. Barnes compares Jesus praying before dawn and through the night (Mark 1:35; Luke 6:12). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Matthew Henry: someone who prays a lot will have a lot to give thanks for. Henry stresses that David got up to do it, perhaps in the cold and dark, rather than giving thanks lying down. It was private thanks, not something done to be seen. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-62.html
- Calvin: getting up at midnight shows how strongly he wanted it. Plenty of people agree with God's law outwardly, but it is real progress to accept it gladly and thank God for it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-62.html
- On "righteous judgments": Gill mentions Aben Ezra's view that these are God's judgments on the wicked who robbed the psalmist, and recalls that the Egyptian firstborn died at midnight. Gill himself prefers to read them as God's word and its just precepts. Poole and Benson likewise take "judgments" to mean God's laws. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) mention Hengstenberg's view that the verse alludes to the Passover midnight (Exodus 12:29). JFB prefer to read it as the psalmist's own night-time prayer and praise, like Paul and Silas (Acts 16:25). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm

**v. 63:** Benson: he was a companion of everyone who feared God, including the poorest, whose company other princes looked down on. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: he is on close, friendly terms with all who fear God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm

**v. 64:** Benson: God meets the needs of all people and creatures out of his goodness. Still, the psalmist values spiritual blessings most, which is why he asks to be taught. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: God's loving-kindness can be seen everywhere on earth (compare Psalm 33:5). Out of that fullness the psalmist asks for the inner teaching of God's word as the greatest mercy of all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-62.htm

**v. 65:** Keil & Delitzsch: in the Teth section the psalmist looks back over his life and sees God's kind purpose in everything that happened to him. God's good word is the source of all good, and it is learned by being humbled. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm

**v. 66:** Precept Austin: "good judgment" (*tuwb ta'am*) literally means good "taste," which by extension means discernment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary
- Keil & Delitzsch: *ta'am* is the ability to tell good from evil, almost by touch. Because he holds on to God's commandments in faith, he can ask confidently for discernment and knowledge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm

**v. 67:** Barnes: "went astray" means wandering, erring or sinning. Prosperity hadn't led him to God, and affliction brought him back. Afflictions are "among the most precious means of grace," though the good may come later rather than at the time (Hebrews 12:11). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Matthew Poole: he did not leave God on purpose or out of contempt. He drifted through weakness and carelessness during good times, like a lost sheep (v. 176). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Geneva Study Bible: the purpose of God's rod is to call us home to him. It compares Jeremiah's image of an untamed calf. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: "word" here means God's word as a duty laid on him, not as a promise. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Both JFB and the Cambridge Bible say the verse can apply to Israel as a nation, disciplined by the exile, or to one person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- The Taw Study Bible on BibleHub: affliction is not always punishment for a specific sin, but God does use a father's discipline to correct his children. https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-67.htm

**v. 68:** Benson: God is good in his nature and does good to everyone, even when he afflicts. Being taught God's statutes is the good the psalmist wants most. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: God is "good" in his attitude toward people and "does good" in acting it out. The psalmist asks this God to be his teacher. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm

**v. 69:** Keil & Delitzsch: the Hebrew verb means to smear or plaster over. The slanderers covered up his real character as if with false whitewash, turning him into a caricature of himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm

**v. 70:** Keil & Delitzsch: a heart covered with fat is a picture of numbness and stubbornness (compare Psalm 17:10; Isaiah 6:10), closed to God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): the proud are so full of the world that they become senseless and complacent. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- The Homilist (in the Biblical Illustrator): "fat as grease" means numb to moral motives, as if sin had deadened the soul's moral nerves. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html

**v. 71:** Calvin: it did him good to be humbled by God's discipline, because it softened him and brought him back to obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html
- Matthew Henry: David spoke from experience. Affliction taught him lessons he would otherwise have missed, and the one who disciplined him also taught him. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html
- Benson: he repeats the thought of v. 67 because it is important, and because the world sees affliction as the worst of evils. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html
- Spurgeon (in the Biblical Illustrator): affliction is not good for everyone, and when it fails the fault lies with the person, not the trial. For believers it cures inner faults, wakes up a sleepy faith, and serves as a dark schoolroom where God's grace is the only light. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the nation learned God's statutes through the Babylonian exile, and individuals learn them through their own trials. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html
- Precept Austin: "that I may learn" states the purpose. Affliction is God's schoolmaster, shaping us more and more into the likeness of his Son. https://www.preceptaustin.org/psalm-119-commentary

**v. 72:** Guzik: if trouble is worth it because it teaches God's word, then that word is also worth more than riches. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Keil & Delitzsch: the word from God's mouth is now more precious to him than the greatest earthly wealth. They credit this to the "school of affliction." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm
- Constable: affliction taught him to value God's statutes more than before (vv. 71–72). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html

**vv. 75–77:** Guzik: because he has paid attention to God's word, the psalmist can say God's judgments are right even while he himself is suffering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Chuck Smith, on v. 75: God disciplines his children because he loves them too much to let them get away with wrongdoing. To say "in faithfulness You have afflicted me" is to admit that what God did was right. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-62.html

**vv. 78–80:** Guzik contrasts the proud with those who fear God. He says the proud had reason to fear the psalmist's prayers, and gives examples: David's prayer against Ahithophel, Hezekiah's against Assyria, and Esther's fast against Haman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/

**vv. 81–82:** Constable: the poet had almost given up waiting for God to save him from his enemies, but he found God's revelation a dependable source of strength. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html
- Coffman reads v. 82, "my eyes fail," as eyesight worn out by long, intense study of God's word. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html
- Ellicott suggests "eyes failing" may simply be another way of saying weeping. https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-83.htm

**v. 83:** Most writers take the image as a picture of misery.
- Barnes: bottles in the East were made of skins and hung in smoky tents. They turned dark and dingy, a symbol of distress. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- JFB: he was withered by sorrow like a skin bottle shrivelled in smoke. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- Poole: his natural moisture was dried up, and he was withered and despised. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- Gill: the image covers both his state of mind (darkness, feeling God had hidden his face, feeling empty and useless) and his body (pale and wrinkled from care and age). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- Matthew Henry: a smoke-wrinkled bottle gets thrown aside, because nobody puts wine in it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html
- Calvin's commentary (as shown on the page) mentions both the blackness and the shrinking. Long suffering wears away a person's beauty and strength in the same way. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html
- Spurgeon: the smoke keeps rising for a long time, so some believers hang in trouble for months. A trial you don't feel can't make you holy, so there is no shame in being sensitive under suffering. Real patience is trusting God while you feel the pain. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html
- **A minority reading, which most writers reject:** some writers point to the ancient custom of mellowing wine in smoke. On that reading, suffering ripens character. Samuel Cox held this view (cited in the Pulpit sermon notes), and Ellicott and the Cambridge Bible mention it. The Cambridge Bible rejects it because the image clearly describes bad effects. Keil & Delitzsch say the custom adds nothing, and the sermon notes doubt it fits the mood of the stanza. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm ; https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/119-83.htm
- **Translation note:** the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) and the Latin Vulgate read "hoar-frost" instead of "smoke." Ellicott notes the Hebrew word means frost in Psalm 148:8 but smoke in Genesis 19:28. The Cambridge Bible says the frost rendering deserves no weight. https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-83.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch (following Hitzig): the picture is of a man set aside in his dungeon and constantly exposed to his persecutors' abuse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm
- A modern application piece on BibleHub: the shrivelled skin still hangs there. It is worn out but not broken, and staying "soaked" in Scripture keeps the soul from cracking. https://biblehub.com/q/Symbolism_of_wineskin_in_smoke.htm

**v. 84:** Guzik: this is one of the few verses in the psalm that doesn't mention God's word. He suggests the psalmist's weakness and sense of injustice have briefly pulled his focus away from it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Constable: feeling like a shrivelled wineskin, he asks how much longer he must wait to be saved (vv. 83–86). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-83.html

**vv. 85–87:** Matthew Henry (Concise): his enemies used cunning as well as force, with contempt for God's law. God's commandments are faithful guides to peace and safety. We can best expect God's help when, like Christ, we do good and suffer for it. The wicked may almost destroy the believer, but he would give up everything rather than God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm

**v. 88:** Guzik, connecting this verse with v. 159: revival is never deserved or earned. It comes from God's loving-kindness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-119/
- Matthew Henry (Concise): we need God's grace for the strength to do good. The surest sign of God's good will toward us is his good work in us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-83.htm

## 2. Where Protestant traditions differ
I found no source showing a real split between denominations on these verses. The writers I read cut across traditions: Calvin, Gill (Baptist), Henry (Nonconformist), Barnes (Presbyterian), Spurgeon (Baptist) and Benson (Methodist). All of them read the affliction verses (67, 71, 75) the same way, as God's fatherly, corrective discipline. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/119-71.html

## 3. Other views
- **vv. 67 and 71, older translations:** the Septuagint and Vulgate read "humbled" rather than "afflicted" (Barnes). The Catholic Douay-Rheims follows this ("Before I was humbled I offended"; "thou hast humbled me"). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/119-67.htm ; https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-71.htm
- **v. 71, older scholarship on the setting:** Ellicott thinks the discipline of the nation is probably meant, and notes that "the uses of adversity" was a common saying among ancient moralists (he cites Aeschylus). https://biblehub.com/psalms/119-71.htm
